claims.text: A machine-learning-driven framework can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr.
Incorporating atomistic disorder, local force-constant fluctuations, and ab initio electronic scattering will improve thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy.
The proposed framework will predict experimental thermal conductivities within ±10%.
The framework can model both defect-free HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
A first-principles-informed machine-learning interatomic potential can independently quantify phonon scattering caused by local disorder and mass fluctuations.
Ab initio electronic-structure calculations can independently evaluate electronic scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen has a measured total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Disorder-induced local force-constant and mass-distribution variations mediate phonon scattering.
Detailed electronic-structure parameters provide a basis for evaluating electronic scattering processes.
Using a machine-learning potential bypasses oversimplified Debye-temperature approximations by capturing atomic-scale disorder and local variations.
Separating lattice and electronic transport channels enables more accurate predictions of each contribution.
Below 200 K, the model will predict nearly equal lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
From 300 to 1200 K, the summed predicted conductivity for oxygen-containing specimens will be 10–17 W/(K·m).
Earlier models rely on DFT-derived elastic properties and Debye-temperature-dependent analytical estimates.
Earlier models assume defect-free crystals and conflate phonon and electronic thermal transport.
The predictive improvement applies to HfNbTaTiZr and similar refractory high-entropy alloys at the specified temperatures and oxygen levels up to approximately 1 wt.%.
The framework may lose accuracy when unmodeled scattering mechanisms dominate or when compositions differ substantially.
